"I have but one tipi. It has but four poles. . . my east lodge pole touches the ground at the Black Hills, my south, the ground at the headwaters of the Wind River, my west, the snow-capped Absaroke and Beartooth Range, the north lodge pole resting on the Bearpaw Mountains."
Government of the Tribe was led by men who had attained the status of chief through accomplishment of four deeds: leadership of a successful war party; stealing picketed horses from an enemy camp; stealing the weapon from an enemy; and counting coup, or being the first to touch or slap an enemy. Men who had performed these deeds were allowed to attend the council of chiefs, and one member of the council was designated head of camp. The council and head of camp served mainly as the authority for selecting another camp site, deciding when to move, and designating various warrior societies to act as camp police. The societies' main function in those days was to guarantee a successful communal buffalo hunt.
At about this time the Crow Tribe consisted of three geographic divisions. The area between the Missouri and Yellowstone Rivers was the home of the River Crows; the lands to the south (between the Big Horn and Wind River Mountains) were occupied by the more numerous Mountain Crows (main body) and the Kicked in the Bellies, (the latter being more closely associated with Mountain Crows). Although it is rather unclear as to why the people were so divided, the divisions did unite for common defense purposes. Never-the-less, the Crows referred to themselves as 'We People'.
